items.title: [Bug]: runai_streamer multi-node: aux (non-tensor) files are not pulled on peer nodes
items.body:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text ============================== System Info ============================== OS : Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS (x86_64) ============================== PyTorch Info ============================== PyTorch version : 2.11.0+cu130 CUDA used to build PyTorch : 13.0 ============================== CUDA / GPU Info ============================== Is CUDA available : True CUDA runtime version : 13.0.88 GPU models and configuration : GPU 0-7: NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 Nvidia driver version : 580.126.20 ============================== Versions of relevant libraries ============================== [pip3] torch==2.11.0+cu130 [pip3] transformers==5.8.0 [pip3] triton==3.6.0 [pip3] nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.28.9 ============================== vLLM Info ============================== vLLM Version : 0.25.1 # Deployment: Ray Serve LLM, 2 x 8xH100 nodes, tensor_parallel_size=16, # load_format=runai_streamer, model_source=az://models/Kimi-K2.5 # (Kimi-K2.5, multimodal + trust_remote_code). # Image: rayproject/ray-llm:nightly.260723.27d78f-py312-cu130 ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug With `--load-format runai_streamer` and a remote object-store model (eg s3, az, gs), weights (that are `*.safetensors` files) stream per-rank into GPU memory, but the smaller non-tensor files (`config.json`, tokenizer, remote-code `*.py`, `*.model`) are pulled to a node-local directory which `model_config.model` points to. That pull runs **only on the driver process**. So on a multi-node deployment, ranks on other nodes get the resolved path but the files were never pulled there, so their directory is empty. Any per-rank code that reads `model_config.model` — **multimodal processors** or **`trust_remote_code` tokenizers** — fails on those nodes. Single-node deployments are fine (all ranks share the driver's dir). ### Root cause https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/config/model.py#L980-L986 `vllm/config/model.py` — the pull happens in `ModelConfig.__post_init__`, which runs where the config is built (the driver), not on the workers: ```python # maybe_pull_model_tokenizer_for_runai object_storage_model = ObjectStorageModel(url=model) object_storage_model.pull_files(model, allow_pattern=["*.model", "*.py", "*.json"]) self.model_weights = model # remote URI -> streamed per-rank (works OK) self.model = object_storage_model.dir # node-local dir -> shared to all ranks ``` The dir is a [deterministic hash of the URL](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/transformers_utils/runai_utils.py#L62-L66), so every node computes the same path but only the driver pulls the files into it. For Driver: builds the  ModelConfig  →  __post_init__  runs →  pull_files  writes 15 files to  .../d7477be7 . Path and files both exist. For Peer: receives the config pickled (already built)  __post_init__  does not re-run →  pull_files  never fires. It gets  self.model = ".../d7477be7"  — the path string — but that dir is empty/absent on its own disk. ### Reproduce A multimodal or `trust_remote_code` model via `runai_streamer` from object storage, with TP spanning more than one node: ```bash vllm serve s3:/// \ --load-format runai_streamer \ --trust-remote-code \ --tensor-parallel-size 16 # > GPUs-per-node, so TP spans 2+ nodes ``` The peer-node rank fails building the multimodal processor (`kimi_k25.py:120`), reading the empty asset dir: ```text (EngineCore pid=9628) EngineCore failed to start. ray.exceptions.RayTaskError(OSError): ray::RayWorkerProc.initialize_worker() (pid=911, ip=10.244.5.125) File ".../vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py", line 398, in init_device self.model_runner = GPUModelRunnerV1(self.vllm_config, self.device) File ".../vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py", line 517, in __init__ self.supports_mm_inputs = self.mm_registry.supports_multimodal_inputs(...) File ".../vllm/model_executor/models/kimi_k25.py", line 120, in __init__ image_processor = cached_get_image_processor(...) File ".../huggingface_hub/utils/_validators.py", line 132, in validate_repo_id raise HFValidationError(...) huggingface_hub.errors.HFValidationError: Repo id must be in the form 'repo_name' or 'namespace/repo_name': '/home/ray/.cache/vllm/assets/model_streamer/d7477be7'. ``` Same hash path `model_streamer/d7477be7` on both nodes, but: ```text # Driver node: 15 files (config.json, tokenization_kimi.py, kimi_k25_vision_processing.py, # preprocessor_config.json, tiktoken.model, modeling_kimi_k25.py, ...) # Peer node: directory does not exist (0 files) ``` ### Proposed fix Re-pull the small non-tensor files on **every node**, before the model runner is built. Add `ModelConfig.maybe_pull_model_files_for_runai_worker()` (re-pulls `*.json` / `*.py` / `*.model` to the node-local dir, guarded by a per-node lock + an idempotent "already pulled?" check), and call it at the **start of the worker's `init_device()`** — which runs on every rank, before `GPUModelRunnerV1.__init__` builds the multimodal processor. Weights still stream per-rank. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: Kimi-K3 FP8 KV Cache configuration error
items.body:
### Your current environment

N/A

### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Steps to reproduce ##

Using the recipe from [recipes.vllm.ai](https://recipes.vllm.ai/moonshotai/Kimi-K3?hardware=b300&features=reasoning%2Ctext_only):
```bash
vllm serve moonshotai/Kimi-K3   \
--trust-remote-code   \
--moe-backend auto   \
--gpu-memory-utilization 0.95   \
--tensor-parallel-size 8   \
--load-format fastsafetensors   \
--no-enable-flashinfer-autotune   \
--max-model-len 1048576   \
--kv-cache-dtype fp8   \
--attention-config '{"use_prefill_query_quantization":true}'   \
--enable-prefix-caching   \
--reasoning-parser kimi_k3   \
--language-model-only
```

## Unexpected behavior ##

vLLM raises an error from [vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/mla.py](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/82ae4164ee016d4daecd2033c26f5c0827984a80/vllm/models/kimi_k3/nvidia/mla.py#L696-L699) claiming that `use_prefill_query_quantization` is not enabled, despite it being enabled 
```
'Kimi-K3 fp8 KV cache requires an fp8 prefill query; enable --attention-config '{"use_prefill_query_quantization": true}'.'

### 🐛 Describe the bug On a single node with multiple Intel Arc Pro B60 GPUs (Battlemage G21, PCI ID `8086:e211`), vLLM **main** (`v0.26.1rc1.dev130+ge04a30a77`) with the current torch 2.13 XPU wheel stack hangs during engine startup at the first TP `all_reduce` (warmup/profile run). The xe driver reports GuC job timeouts and engine resets; all ranks then fail with `UR_RESULT_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST (20)`. Both TP=4 and TP=8 are affected, fp8 and bf16, eager and compiled. The same model/config/hardware works on **vLLM 0.26.0 + torch 2.12** wheels (which bundle oneCCL 2021.17.2). isolated this below vLLM: it is an **oneCCL 2022.x regression**, reproduced with a 15-line pure `torch.distributed` (`xccl`) script — full analysis, minimal reproducer, and per-size matrix in https://github.com/uxlfoundation/oneCCL/issues/215 - oneCCL **2021.17.2** (torch 2.12 wheels): all allreduce sizes pass at full speed. - oneCCL **2022.0.0 / 2022.1.1** (torch 2.13 wheels): messages **≤16 MiB pass at parity**, messages **≥20 MiB hang the GPUs** (cliff at `CCL_SYCL_ALLREDUCE_MEDIUM_THRESHOLD`). vLLM's default warmup dummies `max_num_batched_tokens=8192` tokens → 8192×3584×2 B ≈ **56 MiB** allreduce → hang, before serving a single request. - Downgrading is blocked by an ABI wall: `oneccl==2021.17.2` needs `libsycl.so.8`, torch 2.13 links `libsycl.so.9`. - `CCL_ALLREDUCE=ring` avoids the hang but is ~4–7× slower on the collective — ~30% end-to-end decode regression (~21–22 vs ~31–32 tok/s, TP=4). The ≤16 MiB message-size workaround (`--max-num-batched-tokens 2048`, i.e. ≤14 MiB for hidden 3584) should keep warmup on the healthy path but is an awful bandaid solution. ### Environment | Item | Value | |---|---| | GPUs | 8× Intel Arc Pro B60 24 GB (`8086:e211`), PCIe-only, P2P via `pci=disable_acs_redir=`, `amd_iommu=off` | | Board / CPU | ASRock X870 Pro-A WiFi (AM5), Ryzen 9 9900X | | OS / kernel | Ubuntu 26.04, `7.1.3-070103-generic`, xe driver | | Level Zero | `libze-intel-gpu1 26.27.39122.11-0`, `libze1 1.32.0` | | Broken stack | vLLM main, torch 2.13, `intel-sycl-rt 2026.0.0/2026.1.1`, `oneccl 2022.0.0/2022.1.1`, vllm-xpu-kernels 0.12.0 | | Working stack | vLLM 0.26.0, torch 2.12, `intel-sycl-rt 2025.3.2`, `oneccl 2021.17.2`, vllm-xpu-kernels 0.11.1 | | Model | Gemma-4 31B multimodal (`gemma4_mm`), fp8 and bf16 | ### Repro ```bash vllm serve --tensor-parallel-size 4 # hangs at warmup/profile_run # also with: --max-num-batched-tokens 2048 (multimodal: still hangs) # works, ~30% slower: CCL_ALLREDUCE=ring vllm serve ... ``` ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

The root cause is that nvidia/NV-Embed-v2's `configuration_nvembed.py` has `from transformers.models.auto import CONFIG_MAPPING` as a **module-level import**. When the config object is pickled, this `_LazyConfigMapping` reference is serialized as part of the module's globals. On the child side, `_LazyConfigMapping.__init__` is called without its required `mapping` positional argument during unpickling. As @youkaichao diagnosed in #11055, the model-repo-side fix is to move `from transformers.models.auto import CONFIG_MAPPING` inside the function/method that uses it (in this case, `NVEmbedConfig.__init__`). However, this is a recurring issue across many `trust_remote_code` models — vLLM should either handle it robustly or document the requirement clearly. ### How to Reproduce ```bash vllm serve nvidia/NV-Embed-v2 \ --trust-remote-code ``` Crashes at startup before model loading. Reproduces on any backend (GPU, CPU, etc.) with vLLM's V1 engine (multiprocessing mode). Not platform-specific. **Note:** Also requires the fix for `LlamaBidirectionalConfig.verify_and_update_model_config` accessing `hf_config.pooling` without `getattr` (separate issue — without that fix, startup crashes earlier with an `AttributeError`). ### Stack Trace ``` Traceback (most recent call last): File "", line 1, in File "/opt/conda/lib/python3.12/multiprocessing/spawn.py", line 122, in spawn_main exitcode = _main(fd, parent_sentinel) File "/opt/conda/lib/python3.12/multiprocessing/spawn.py", line 132, in _main self = reduction.pickle.load(from_parent) TypeError: _LazyConfigMapping.__init__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'mapping' RuntimeError: Engine core initialization failed. See root cause above. Failed core proc(s): {} ``` ### Expected Behavior The engine core subprocess should start and proceed to model loading. Custom HF configs loaded via `trust_remote_code` should serialize correctly across the V1 engine's multiprocessing boundary. ### Environment - **vLLM**: 0.24.0 - **Python**: 3.12.11 - **torch**: 2.6.x - **transformers**: latest (loads custom NVEmbedConfig from model repo) ### Context - **Regression?**: NO — NV-Embed-v2 never worked with V1 engine - **Affected models**: nvidia/NV-Embed-v2 (and any `trust_remote_code` model whose config.py has `from transformers.models.auto import CONFIG_MAPPING` at module level) - **Related issues/PRs**: - #11055 — Identical root cause (`_LazyConfigMapping` pickle failure with V1 + custom models). @youkaichao diagnosed the fix: move `CONFIG_MAPPING` import inside the function. Closed but still affecting users. - #5826 — Original report of `NVEmbedModel` not supported (closed as stale, never resolved) - #15849 — NV-Embed-v2 support request (closed as stale) ### Root Cause Detail In nvidia/NV-Embed-v2's [`configuration_nvembed.py`](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NV-Embed-v2/blob/main/configuration_nvembed.py): ```python # Module-level import — causes the pickle failure from transformers.models.auto import CONFIG_MAPPING ``` `CONFIG_MAPPING` is a `_LazyConfigMapping` instance. When Python pickles the `NVEmbedConfig` object (which references this module), `_LazyConfigMapping` gets serialized. On deserialization, `_LazyConfigMapping.__init__()` is invoked without the `mapping` argument it requires — hence the TypeError. ### Suggested Fix **vLLM-side robustness** Make V1 engine config serialization robust to unpicklable HF config objects: 1. Serialize `hf_config` as `hf_config.to_dict()` + `model_name_or_path` before sending to child 2. In child, reconstruct via `AutoConfig.from_pretrained(model_path, trust_remote_code=True)` This would fix the entire class of `CONFIG_MAPPING`-at-module-level issues across all affected models, not just NV-Embed-v2. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: # Bug: `Maximum concurrency` startup log contradicts `/metrics` endpoint due to premature `block_size` resolution
items.body:
## Bug: Startup log `Maximum concurrency` contradicts `/metrics` `kv_cache_max_concurrency`

### My current environment

```text
vLLM version: 0.26.0
Model: nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-NVFP4 (284B MoE, DeepseekV4ForCausalLM)
Hardware: 2× Blackwell (SM120), 96 GB each
TP=2, EP enabled
KV cache dtype: fp8
KV connector: SimpleCPUOffloadConnector (50 GiB CPU per rank)
Max model len: 262,144
Block size: 256
Prefix caching: enabled
```

### How to reproduce

```bash
vllm serve nvidia/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-NVFP4 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
  --enable-expert-parallel \
  --max-model-len 262144 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.936 \
  --block-size 256 \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"SimpleCPUOffloadConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"cpu_bytes_to_use_per_rank":53687091200}}'
```

### The problem

The `Maximum concurrency` value printed in the startup log disagrees with the `kv_cache_max_concurrency` label in the `/metrics` endpoint.

**Startup log:**
```
GPU KV cache size: 302,945 tokens
Maximum concurrency for 262,144 tokens per request: 1.16x
```

**`/metrics` endpoint:**
```
vllm:cache_config_info{
  kv_cache_max_concurrency="0.47086269282041515",
  kv_cache_size_tokens="123433",
  num_gpu_blocks="14835",
  ...
} 1.0
```

| Source | kv_cache_size_tokens | Concurrency |
|---|---|---|
| Startup log | 302,945 | 1.16x |
| `/metrics` | 123,433 | 0.47x |

Both use the same formula (`num_blocks / sum(blocks_per_group)`) but with different inputs — the startup log is computed during `get_kv_cache_configs()` on a per-worker config, while `/metrics` reflects a later config sent via `EngineCoreReadyResponse`. It is unclear which value corresponds to the config the scheduler actually enforces.

### Expected behavior

The two values should agree. Whichever config the scheduler actually runs with should be used for both the startup log and the `/metrics` label.

### Root cause

`get_kv_cache_configs()` in `vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py` (line ~2197) computes and logs the concurrency **per-worker** using each worker's full `available_memory`:

```python
for kv_cache_config in kv_cache_configs:
    kv_cache_config.num_blocks = min_num_blocks
    ...
    num_tokens, max_concurrency = get_kv_cache_capacity(vllm_config, kv_cache_config)
    logger.info_once("GPU KV cache size: %s tokens", f"{num_tokens:,}")
    logger.info_once("Maximum concurrency for %s tokens per request: %.2fx",
                     f"{max_model_len:,}", max_concurrency)
```

The `EngineCoreReadyResponse` sent to the API server carries a different `KVCacheConfig` with `num_blocks=14835`, which is what `/metrics` exposes. The log message is emitted on the first config and never updated to match the final one.

### Suggested fix

Ensure the startup log and the `/metrics` label are computed from the same `KVCacheConfig` — either log after finalization, or log both values.

items.title: [Bug]: vLLM 0.26.0 incompatible with transformers 5.x (5.14.1) Qwen3.6-35B-A3B  config class renaming
items.body:
### Your current environment PyTorch version: >= 2.6.0 CUDA version: 12.6 (training) / cu130 (serve via vLLM) NCCL version: 2.18.1 cuDNN version: 8.8.0 TensorRT version: Not installed NumPy version: 1.24.3 PyYAML version: 6.0 vLLM version: 0.26.0 Transformers version: 5.14.1 Platform: Linux (GCP VM, not AWS) NVIDIA GPU: 4× NVIDIA L4 (22GB each) GPU compute capability: sm_89 ### 🐛 Describe the bug ## Problem vLLM 0.26.0 fails to load Qwen3.6-35B-A3B models when using transformers 5.x because of a config class mismatch. **Error:** Expected type: but found type: 
```python
from vllm import LLM
model = LLM("Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B", dtype="float16")

You get this error:

TypeError: Invalid type of HuggingFace config. 
Expected type: <class 'vllm.transformers_utils.configs.qwen3_5_moe.Qwen3_5MoeConfig'> 
but found type: <class 'transformers.models.qwen3_5_moe.configuration_qwen3_5_moe.Qwen3_5MoeTextConfig'>

Root Cause

transformers 5.x renamed Qwen3.5-MoE config classes:

transformers Version | Config Class Name -- | -- < 5.0 | Qwen3_5MoeConfig >= 5.0 | Qwen3_5MoeTextConfig (text-only) >= 5.0 | Qwen3_5MoeVisionConfig (vision) >= 5.0 | Qwen3_5MoeConfig (multimodal wrapper)

The problem:

  • When a model is trained with transformers 5.3.0+, its config.json contains "model_type": "qwen3_5_moe_text"
  • transformers loads this as Qwen3_5MoeTextConfig
  • But vLLM's config registry expects Qwen3_5MoeConfig
  • Type checking at vllm/transformers_utils/config.py fails

Steps to Reproduce

# Requirements:
# - vLLM >= 0.26.0
# - transformers >= 5.0.0
# - A Qwen3.5-MoE model (e.g., Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B)

from vllm import LLM

try:
    model = LLM(
        "Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B",
        dtype="float16",
        tensor_parallel_size=1
    )
except TypeError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")
    # Error: Invalid type of HuggingFace config...

Expected Behavior

✅ Model should load successfully regardless of whether transformers uses the old or new config class names.

Actual Behavior

❌ TypeError thrown due to config class mismatch.

Environment

  • vLLM: 0.26.0
  • transformers: 5.0.0+
  • Model: Qwen3.5-MoE (any variant)
  • Python: 3.10+

Additional Context

The issue is specific to models that:

  1. Are trained/fine-tuned with transformers >= 5.0.0
  2. Use the new Qwen3_5MoeTextConfig class name in their config
  3. Are loaded with vLLM 0.26.0 which hasn't been updated to recognize the new class names

All 32 lanes fault together, i.e. the whole tile's base pointer is bad rather than a tail element being over-read. The faulting address sits ~90 GB below the other live pointers. ### Where the int32 comes from `vllm/v1/attention/backends/flex_attention.py` builds `kv_indices` as int32 (still true on `main` as of 2026-07-30): ```python kv_indices = unique_static_unsorted((used_pages_padded.long()), M=self.num_blocks).to(torch.int32) kv_indices = copy_to_persistent(self.persistent_kv_indices, kv_indices) self.persistent_kv_indices = torch.empty( self.max_num_query_groups, self.max_num_kv_indices, dtype=torch.int32, device=self.device) ``` so every downstream term stays in that dtype (`kv_start = kv_indices * block_size`, `ptr = K + offs_n * stride_kn`). The generated kernel does define `INDEX_DTYPE = tl.int64`, but only the **output store** indices go through it; the K/V gather offsets do not. What makes the offset exceed the K tensor's own `numel` is that **K and V share one buffer**, so the K view's maximum linear offset spans the *whole* buffer while its `numel` is only half of it. Inductor appears to pick the index dtype from `numel` (~1.12e9 here, which fits int32) rather than from the stride-derived maximum offset (~2.24e9, which does not). ⚠️ **The packing axis differs between releases — this needs updating before submitting.** Our environment (`0.23.1rc1.dev813+g344609ab1`) packs on a dedicated dim and splits with `unbind`: ```python # flex_attention.py:133 (dev813, what we measured) return (num_blocks, 2, block_size, num_kv_heads, head_size) # flex_attention.py:1245 / :1350 key_cache, value_cache = kv_cache.unbind(1) ``` `main` (2026-07-30) packs into the content dim instead: ```python # K and V are packed into the content dim: logical (B, H, N, 2*hs). return (num_blocks, num_kv_heads, block_size, 2 * head_size) ... kv_cache = kv_cache.transpose(1, 2) key_cache, value_cache = kv_cache.split(hs, dim=-1) ``` The bound is **unchanged** by this, because in both layouts the buffer holds `num_blocks * block_size * (2 * num_kv_heads * head_size)` elements and the K view's maximum offset reaches the far end of it: ``` max_safe_num_gpu_blocks = 2**31 // (block_size * 2 * num_kv_heads * head_size) = 2**31 // (16 * 2 * 8 * 128) = 65,536 ``` but the *per-token* stride differs, so **the `main` derivation above is analytical — we measured the `unbind` layout, not the packed one.** Re-run snippet (b) against `main`'s layout before filing. Bisecting one property at a time on the layout we did measure, the shared buffer is the only necessary condition: replacing the two strided views with separate contiguous K/V tensors halves the stride and doubles the bound. `kv_indices` contiguity, Q layout, `enable_gqa`, `Q_LEN` alignment and `KV_LEN` magnitude are all irrelevant. Also note `kv_cache_utils.py` now has a `_use_packed_kv_cache_config` / `_get_packed_kv_cache_layout` path returning a `block_stride`; whether that changes the effective stride for this backend is **not checked**. ### Who is exposed `num_blocks = available_memory // (group_size * page_size)` where `group_size = max(len(g.layer_names) for g in kv_cache_groups)` — the number of memory pools the hybrid allocator creates. **Exposure grows as `group_size` shrinks**, so models whose layers split into many KV cache groups are the most exposed; a uniform single-group model needs proportionally more memory to reach the bound. Being upfront about our own trigger: we reached `num_gpu_blocks = 70,315` with an **out-of-tree** backend whose per-layer window config split 36 layers into 4 groups (`group_size = 9`, 37.56 GiB of KV cache). The same 36 layers as a single group give only ~17,579 blocks. So this is not straightforward to reproduce with a stock uniform model on one 80 GB card — hence snippet (b), which exercises the kernel-level mechanism directly and needs neither vLLM nor weights. In memory terms the bound is `4 GiB * group_size` of KV cache per pool group (bf16, this layout). Two-mode summary: | condition | result | | --- | --- | | block id < bound | correct | | block id ≥ bound, wrapped address unmapped | `CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered` | | block id ≥ bound, wrapped address **mapped** | **no error — silently reads the neighbouring allocation, wrong output** | Consistent with a latent bound rather than a workload issue: everything that appeared to "fix" it — lowering `gpu_memory_utilization`, capping `max_num_seqs`, enabling eviction, `PYTORCH_NO_CUDA_MEMORY_CACHING=1` — merely keeps the allocator from handing out block ids at the top of the pool. ### Upstream status The int32 offset arithmetic itself lives in PyTorch's generated FlexAttention kernel and **has since been fixed**: [pytorch#190857](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/190857) (closed) and [PR #185264](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/185264), which adds an `INDEX_DTYPE` parameter to `load_checked_2d` and casts the offsets before they are multiplied by strides, at every call site in the forward, backward and common templates. So on a torch that carries #185264 this should no longer be reachable, even with int32 `kv_indices`. It remains reachable on releases without it — ours (`2.11.0+cu128`) has `INDEX_DTYPE` appearing zero times in `torch/_inductor/kernel/flex/templates/utilities.py.jinja`. ### Suggested mitigations on the vLLM side 1. **Validate at start-up** (cheap, no perf impact): warn or clamp when `num_gpu_blocks` exceeds `2**31 // (block_size * kv_packing * num_kv_heads * head_size)` and the running torch lacks the fix. We do this out-of-tree by wrapping `kv_cache_utils.may_override_num_blocks`; it cost 4.1% of pool capacity (70,315 → 65,536 blocks, 243,350 → 233,263 tokens) with no measurable throughput change, and it removed both failure modes. 2. Or declare a **minimum torch version** for the FlexAttention backend. 3. Optionally, a **non-interleaved** K/V layout for this backend — halving the row stride doubles the bound regardless of the torch version. FWIW the `persistent_rswa_kv_indices` comment in the same file already documents an adjacent hazard ("... producing an out-of-bounds K/V pointer and a CUDA illegal memory access") and fixes it for the R-SWA path only; this report is the non-R-SWA path with a different mechanism. - [x] Searched existing issues (found none covering the int32 index bound; #13824 / #23814 / #33242 / #35706 / #39025 are unrelated illegal-memory-access reports)

items.title: [Bug][PD][Mooncake] Client disconnect on decode node does not release prefill KV cache
items.body:
### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text Your output of `python collect_env.py` here ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug ```markdown ### 🐛 Describe the bug In an online serving deployment using P/D disaggregation with `MooncakeConnector`, a client disconnect or gateway timeout can cancel the request on the decode (D) node before the request is submitted to its `EngineCore`. In this situation, the corresponding prefill (P) request has already completed and its KV cache blocks are retained for the D node to pull. However, the cancellation on D is not propagated to P, so the P-side KV cache blocks remain allocated until `VLLM_MOONCAKE_ABORT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` expires. Under continuous traffic, these orphaned pending transfers accumulate and can exhaust the P node's KV cache, causing subsequent requests to stall. ### Deployment topology ```text Client | v Gateway / PD coordinator | +----> Prefill node (MooncakeConnector, kv_producer) | +----> Decode node (MooncakeConnector, kv_consumer) ``` The frontend uses the OpenAI-compatible online serving API. ### Observed request sequence ```text 1. The gateway sends the request to the P node. 2. The P node completes prefill and retains its KV blocks for transfer. 3. The gateway sends the decode request to the D node. 4. The D node logs `Arrived request `. 5. The client disconnects or the gateway request times out. 6. `with_cancellation` cancels the D-side HTTP handler. 7. The D request is cancelled before `_log_inputs()` and `engine_client.generate()` are reached. 8. Since no D-side EngineCore request was created, `AsyncLLM.generate()` never runs its cancellation path and no abort notification is sent to P. 9. The P node continues retaining the KV blocks until the Mooncake abort timeout. ``` A characteristic symptom is that the D node logs: ```text Arrived request ``` but does not log: ```text Received request ``` The relevant D-side code path is: ```text create_chat_completion() -> _log_arrival() -> render_chat_request() -> _log_inputs() -> engine_client.generate() ``` The cancellation happens between `_log_arrival()` and `_log_inputs()`. ### Relevant code The HTTP handler is cancelled by `with_cancellation`: ```python handler_task = asyncio.create_task(handler_func(*args, **kwargs)) cancellation_task = asyncio.create_task(listen_for_disconnect(request)) done, pending = await asyncio.wait( [handler_task, cancellation_task], return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED, ) for task in pending: task.cancel() ``` `AsyncLLM.generate()` only aborts a request after a request output collector has been created: ```python except (asyncio.CancelledError, GeneratorExit) as e: if q is not None: await self.abort(q.request_id, internal=True, error=e) ``` In the reported scenario, `engine_client.generate()` has not been reached, so there is no local D request to abort. Mooncake eventually releases unsent P-side blocks using: ```text VLLM_MOONCAKE_ABORT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT ``` The current default is 480 seconds. This prevents permanent retention, but it is too slow to prevent KV cache pressure under repeated client disconnects. Reducing the timeout significantly is risky because it is a fixed timeout: a valid D request may still be queued, performing a handshake, or waiting to start the transfer. Releasing its P-side KV blocks too early may cause a KV load failure or request stall. ### Expected behavior When a decode request is cancelled because of a client disconnect or gateway timeout, the associated P-side pending transfer and retained KV blocks should be released promptly. The solution should also remain safe when the D node is only delayed rather than dead. ### Actual behavior Only the D-side HTTP task is cancelled. The P node is not notified and continues holding the KV blocks until `VLLM_MOONCAKE_ABORT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` expires. Repeated cancellations can accumulate retained P-side blocks and eventually cause the PD serving system to stall because of KV cache exhaustion. ### Why `/abort_requests` does not fully solve this for online serving There is an `/abort_requests` endpoint under the disaggregated serving router, but it is currently registered only when `tokens_only=True`. A normal OpenAI-compatible online server generally runs with `tokens_only=False`, so this endpoint is not available. In addition: 1. The gateway must preserve the mapping between the external request, P request ID, D request ID, and Mooncake `transfer_id`. 2. Calling abort only on D cannot release P-side resources. 3. The P request may already have completed and been removed from normal `OutputProcessor` request mappings while Mooncake still retains its blocks, so aborting by the original request ID after completion may be a no-op. 4. The endpoint starts abort in a background task and returns HTTP 200 before abort completion is known. ### Possible solutions Would the community consider one or more of the following? 1. **Connector-level cancellation by `transfer_id`** Add an explicit Mooncake cancellation API that removes the pending transfer and releases retained P-side blocks, even after the P EngineCore request has completed. 2. **Lease renewal / heartbeat** Add a lease mechanism similar to the NIXL P-side KV block lease: ```text D queued/alive -> heartbeat renews the P-side lease D cancelled/dead -> heartbeat stops -> P releases blocks ``` This would distinguish a slow but valid D request from an abandoned request more reliably than a fixed timeout. 3. **PD coordinator cancellation propagation** Define an official cancellation workflow in which the coordinator tracks: ```text external request ID -> P request ID -> D request ID -> transfer_id ``` A client disconnect would then fan out cancellation to both P and D. 4. **Expose a guarded abort endpoint for online serving** Allow `/abort_requests` or a connector-specific abort endpoint to be enabled independently of `tokens_only`, with explicit authentication/security controls. 5. **Ensure cancellation cleanup is awaited** After `handler_task.cancel()`, await the cancelled task so that any cancellation cleanup in `finally` blocks is completed before returning. ### Reproduction steps 1. Start a P node and D node with `MooncakeConnector`. 2. Send a request through a PD-aware gateway. 3. Wait until the P node finishes prefill and retains its KV blocks. 4. Send the corresponding request to D. 5. Disconnect the client or trigger a gateway timeout immediately after the D node logs `Arrived request`, but before it logs `Received request`. 6. Repeat this operation under concurrent traffic. 7. Observe that the P-side pending transfers/KV blocks remain until `VLLM_MOONCAKE_ABORT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` and that available KV cache gradually decreases. ### Environment Please fill in the following information: - vLLM version or commit: - Mooncake version: - GPU type: - Number of P nodes: - Number of D nodes: - Tensor parallel size: - Pipeline parallel size: - `kv_transfer_config`: - `VLLM_MOONCAKE_ABORT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT`: - Gateway implementation: - Streaming or non-streaming: - Prefix caching enabled: - Async scheduling enabled: - Reproduction frequency: ### Logs D node: ```text Arrived request # No corresponding "Received request" log ``` P node: ```text # Prefill finishes and blocks are retained. # Blocks are not released until the Mooncake abort timeout. ``` ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

### 🐛 Describe the bug ### Summary This issue aims to report a security-relevant hardening issue in the RayExecutorV2 path. In deployments where a platform or launcher exposes `ray_runtime_env` or an equivalent runtime configuration field to less-trusted tenants, vLLM currently appears to inherit and propagate the caller-controlled Ray `runtime_env` into vLLM model worker processes without sanitizing code-execution-capable fields. This can cause Ray `worker_process_setup_hook` / runtime package fields to be applied inside `RayWorkerProc` processes before vLLM worker initialization and before distributed communication setup. The path is configuration-driven: 1. A less-trusted requester controls only a launch/config JSON field such as `ray_runtime_env`. 2. The requester does not need direct access to Ray internal ports. 3. The requester does not need to submit an arbitrary Ray Python job or modify the platform-owned vLLM launcher function. 4. vLLM inherits the current Ray runtime environment and propagates it into `RayWorkerProc`. 5. Ray applies the inherited setup hook inside the vLLM model worker process before worker init. ### Affected code paths The relevant flow appears to be: 1. `vllm/engine/arg_utils.py` - vLLM reads the current Ray runtime env with `ray.get_runtime_context().runtime_env`. - The same object is later passed into `ParallelConfig` as `ray_runtime_env`. 2. `vllm/v1/executor/ray_utils.py` - `initialize_ray_cluster()` passes `parallel_config.ray_runtime_env` into `ray.init(..., runtime_env=...)`. 3. `vllm/v1/executor/ray_executor_v2.py` - `RayExecutorV2._build_runtime_env()` starts from `self.parallel_config.ray_runtime_env`. - The resulting `runtime_env` is passed into `RayWorkerProc.options(runtime_env=runtime_env)`. I did not find an allowlist or sanitizer for high-risk Ray runtime_env fields such as: - `worker_process_setup_hook` - `working_dir` - `py_modules` - `pip` - `conda` - `container` - `image_uri` - environment variables such as `__RAY_WORKER_PROCESS_SETUP_HOOK_ENV_VAR`, `PYTHONPATH`, `LD_PRELOAD`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` ### Impact This is conditional on an outer platform or launcher exposing `ray_runtime_env` or equivalent runtime configuration to less-trusted users. Under that condition, the impact is code execution in vLLM Ray model worker processes during startup, before vLLM worker initialization and before distributed communication initialization. Potential impact includes: - execution with the privileges of the vLLM/Ray worker process; - reading environment variables, mounted credentials, model/cache paths, or service-side files accessible to the worker; - modifying the worker startup environment; - corrupting model-worker behavior before model load; - denial of service by injecting startup-time behavior into every worker. ### Local validation summary I reproduced this with a marker-writing validation hook on: - vLLM commit: `ee0da84ab9e04ac7610e28580af62c365e898389` (`v0.24.0` in my test logs) - Python: `3.10.20` - Ray: `` - `VLLM_USE_RAY_V2_EXECUTOR_BACKEND=1` - `distributed_executor_backend="ray"` Important observations: **1. Static passthrough** `RayExecutorV2._build_runtime_env()` preserved caller-controlled `runtime_env` fields including `worker_process_setup_hook`, `working_dir`, `py_modules`, and custom `env_vars`. **2. vLLM worker propagation** When vLLM was launched inside a Ray context carrying the runtime_env hook: - the outer Ray task received a marker, which is expected Ray behavior; - a separate marker was also written by the vLLM `RayWorkerProc` process; - vLLM completed a generation request in the single-worker test. This indicates that the runtime_env was not limited to the outer Ray task; it reached the vLLM model worker actor. **3. Restricted JSON launcher test** I also tested a restricted platform-style launcher: - caller-controlled input: JSON only; - fixed server-owned launcher code; - no caller-submitted `ray.remote` function; - no direct caller access to Ray internal ports; - JSON contains model settings and `ray_runtime_env`. The marker hook still reached `RayWorkerProc`. **4. Startup timing** The `RayWorkerProc` marker timestamp was earlier than: - vLLM distributed init log lines such as `parallel_state.py` / `distributed_init_method=...`; - model loading log lines such as `Starting to load model`. This supports that the execution occurs during worker startup via Ray runtime_env, not through distributed communication channels. **5. Patch-control test** I tested a local mitigation that sanitizes runtime_env before both: - `ray.init(..., runtime_env=...)`; and - `RayWorkerProc.options(runtime_env=...)`. With both points sanitized, the outer Ray task marker may still appear as Ray/platform-level behavior, but the `RayWorkerProc` marker disappears. ```text RayWorkerProc pids: [137031] marker pids: [136465] intersection: [] VERDICT: PASS RayWorkerProc hook blocked ``` This suggests the issue is fixable at the vLLM layer for vLLM model workers. ### Expected behavior vLLM should not propagate untrusted or inherited Ray runtime_env fields that can execute code inside model worker processes unless the operator explicitly opts into that behavior. ### Suggested fix Introduce a sanitizer or allowlist before vLLM passes runtime_env to Ray at both entry points: before `ray.init(..., runtime_env=parallel_config.ray_runtime_env)` in `vllm/v1/executor/ray_utils.py`; before `RayWorkerProc.options(runtime_env=runtime_env)` in `vllm/v1/executor/ray_executor_v2.py`. Possible denylist fields: - `worker_process_setup_hook` - `working_dir` - `py_modules` - `pip` - `conda` - `container` - `image_uri` Possible denylisted environment variables: - `__RAY_WORKER_PROCESS_SETUP_HOOK_ENV_VAR` - `PYTHONPATH` - `LD_PRELOAD` - `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` - potentially `PATH` Another option is an explicit unsafe opt-in, for example: - `--allow-unsafe-ray-runtime-env` - `VLLM_ALLOW_UNSAFE_RAY_RUNTIME_ENV=1` Default behavior should be conservative for model worker startup. ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.
